newsitem.title: CHINA: FORECAST-Chinese yuan seen under pressure to rise. [CORRECTED 21:44 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Chinese yuan seen under pressure to rise. [CORRECTED 21:44 GMT]

text.p: The Chinese yuan is under pressure to rise in the coming month due to China's high foreign trade surplus, but expected intervention by the central bank will keep the uptrend under control, analysts said on Sunday.

The Chinese currency is likely to move mainly in a range between 8.2940 and 8.2930, against a range of 8.2950 to 8.2960 against the U.S. dollar on the Shanghai-based China Foreign Exchange Trade system, an interbank market, they said.
The yuan edged up to close at a seven-week high of 8.2949 on Friday.
"China's high foreign trade surplus is likely to push more dollars on to the market, adding to the current oversupply of foreign currency," said a foreign exchange trader.
"The yuan is under heavy pressure to rise," he said.
"Despite an oversupply of dollars on the market, the central bank is expected to keep firm control over the rising momentum of the Chinese yuan," said another trader.
China has announced that its foreign trade surplus was $6.71 billion in the first three months of 1997, against a deficit of $1.1 billion (corrects the currency from yuan) in the same 1996 period.
China's total 1996 foreign trade surplus was $12 billion, official figures show. Analysts said they expected the 1997 surplus to be much higher.

The official Business Daily said in a recent report the yuan was likely to continue to rise in 1997 after three years of consecutive rises due to the surging foreign exchange reserves and foreign trade surplus.

"In 1997, foreign exchange supply will continue to exceed demand, as it has for the past three years," the newspaper quoted an unidentified official with the State Administration of Foreign Exchange as saying.
"The Chinese yuan will face pressure to rise further this year despite three consecutive years of rises," he said.
The yuan rose 0.3 percent in 1996 after a rise of 2.9 percent in 1994 and 1.5 percent in 1995.
By the end of February, China's foreign exchange reserves hit a record high of $111 billion yuan, against $105 billion by the end of 1996 and $31.5 billion by the end of 1995, official figures show.
Analysts said other factors exerting upward pressure on the yuan include the continued flow of foreign investment into China.
Despite the yuan's rises, the People's Bank, the central bank, has consistently intervened in the market to prevent the yuan from surging, market sources said.
"This intervention has been the major reason for the yuan to move mainly in that narrow range of 8.2950/8.5960 in the past month," a foreign exchange analyst said.
The central bank has a seperate trading room on the market which enables it to access all trading details.
Other institutions trading on the market can only see details of their own transactions and so remain in the dark about other trades.
